demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 43, a physical therapist by trade, and she describes her life as having split into “before” and “after” the day a routine work moment went wrong. For years she has built her identity around helping people move again, coaxing strength back into injured bodies with patience and precision. She is practical, calm in emergencies, the one colleagues call when a patient is fearful or frustrated. That is how she sees herself, and it is part of what makes the injury she caused so hard to bear: it happened in the very setting where she had always felt most competent.

The incident occurs during a standard treatment session. She is working with a patient she knows well, and she is focused on helping him progress, believing the exercise is safe. In a fraction of a second, a small miscalculation, a shift in footing, and the patient goes down badly. The outcome is serious and immediate. She remembers the sound more than anything else at first, then the look on his face, then the sudden, stunned silence in the room before the alarm of pain and panic takes over. She calls for help, but she also feels herself freeze, as though her body does not understand what has happened even while her mind is racing ahead to the worst possibilities. She says she knows, rationally, that she did not intend harm, but intent offers no shelter from the instant conviction that she has ruined another person’s life.

In the days that follow, she moves through work and home in a kind of numb, overcontrolled state. She keeps replaying the moment from different angles, searching for the exact point where she could have prevented it. At night she lies awake reconstructing every detail, convincing herself that if she thinks hard enough she will find the mistake and make sense of it. Instead, the memory becomes sharper and more merciless with repetition. She begins to dread anything that resembles the event: the sound of a body hitting the floor, the sight of a treatment table, the quiet before a session starts. At work she becomes hyperaware of every movement she makes. She checks and rechecks instructions, steps, hand placement, patient positioning. What used to come naturally now feels staged and unsafe, as if one wrong decision will have catastrophic consequences.

As the weeks pass, she starts avoiding the parts of her job that remind her most of the injury. She asks to trade certain patients, especially those with falls risk or complex mobility issues. She becomes tense when coworkers suggest handling tasks that require quick physical judgment. She notices herself scanning rooms for hazards, exits, and possible failures before she can even listen to what a patient is saying. Her concentration slips. She loses track of conversations, forgets small details, and feels ashamed by the change because this is the work she once performed so confidently. She worries that others can see what she is thinking, that they can read the guilt in her face and understand that she is dangerous. Even compliments now feel unbearable; when someone tells her she is a good therapist, she hears it as something she has already disproven.

At home, her partner becomes both a comfort and a challenge. He wants to reassure her, but she often cannot take it in. She answers his questions with short, careful replies and then shuts down, exhausted by the effort of holding herself together. She is jumpy when the phone rings, especially if it is from work. She startles at sudden sounds and feels a rush of heat and nausea when she is caught off guard. She has vivid dreams that return her to the treatment room, and she wakes with her heart pounding, already mourning before she is fully awake. There are moments when she feels detached from her own body, as if she is watching herself perform her life from a distance. On harder days, she sits in the car outside work for several minutes before she can make herself go inside.

What troubles her most is not only the memory of the accident but the permanence of responsibility. She keeps returning to the fact that another person was badly hurt, and she cannot separate that reality from her own image of herself. She is not only grieving the event; she is grieving the version of herself who moved through the world without this burden. Even now, long after the injury, she remains caught between wanting to prove she is still capable and fearing that any mistake will confirm the worst thing she believes about herself.
